speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Prime Minister what is the extent to which businesses have been able to benefit from Singapore's COVID-19 financing schemes, which were rolled out to provide them access to credit and improve cash flows, with specifics on (i) total quantum of loans dispersed (ii) number of business loan applications approved (iii) approval rates and (iv) average applicable interest rates, for the period ending 30 April 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is done through the ESG loan schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is about six times the credit extended over the same period last year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Under the ESG loan schemes, the Government takes 90% of the loss if a loan goes bad, with the banks assuming the remaining 10%.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This has helped bring down the credit spread that the banks charged.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The ESG loan schemes were then further enhanced when MAS launched a new Singapore Dollar facility for the banks and finance companies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It provides them with fully collateralised funding for two years at an interest rate of 0.1% per annum, for the purpose of their loans under the ESG schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This funding differs from the existing five-year, uncollateralised funding provided by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We have also seen good take-up of the complementary set of relief measures to help SMEs during this period.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These measures were announced earlier by MAS and the financial industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They include enabling SME borrowers with secured loans to defer principal repayments until 31 December 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As of 30 April 2020, more than 2,500 applications have been processed, with nearly all applications approved.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS and ESG will continue to monitor the effectiveness of our measures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Nevertheless, Minister, amongst the SME circle, the expectations seem to be varying.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many people are focusing that the Government has committed to risk-share at 90% and made cost of fund available at 0.1% for these SME loans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, the feedback so far has been that actually the rates offered by banks have been quite different and they feel that the rate has yet to reflect the Government's support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister for his view – three questions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The loan application volume – yes, we have seen significant increase but it is unusual times, so the loan volume and the interest rate, whether these are in line with the Government's policy intention; is it seeing the volume it expects?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, with 2%-3%, yet Government offering 90% risk-share and 0.1% interest rate, whether SMEs' expectation for lower market interest rates are reasonable?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And third, some SMEs have said the banks' requirements for SMEs to provide personal guarantees are too demanding and not commensurate with the banks' risk exposure; so, whether the Minister thinks these requirements are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, the cost of fund is just one component of an interest rate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Beyond that, there is a credit spread depending on the risk profile of the borrower, and in this case, the Government going to bear 90% of the loan losses, that will bring down the credit spread.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, there is also another component which is the bank's own cost, their administration costs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, if you add up, it would be above 0.1%, which is just the cost of funds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In April, most of the interest rates charged for ESG loans were between 2% and 4.5%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it has come down from before, which was 6% or more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think, it is largely Government measures stepping in to lower cost of funds plus credit spread that have led to this outcome.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether the volume is according to our expectation, it is hard to say.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It all depends on how deep the economic troubles will be.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We certainly do not wish for the volume to be too huge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It means that the economic disruption is bigger, but I think the situation is still fluid.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think our measures are in place to answer to the needs of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the purpose of these ESG loans is to address an unexpected event – a black swan event – that is devastating to the economy and to many industries and firms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to make sure that firms do not just collapse as a result of this event.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are firms that otherwise would have been viable, which is why the Government put in a massive Job Support Scheme (JSS) and at the same time, provide these loans to help companies tide over.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think to be able to pledge your personal assets, is an indication of the confidence of the business owner, that this is actually a viable business and that is worthwhile supporting it to tide through this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question is really in terms of personal guarantees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I suppose just to clarify, would the extent to which banks deploying these ESG loans ask for personal guarantees, does that also – are you seeing that also being reduced because of the 90% Government risk-share?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the second question, I am afraid I do not have the data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, as I explained to Ms Foo Mee Har, the personal guarantee is an indication of the confidence of the business owner on how viable the business is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think it is a necessary prudential measure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since the Global Financial Crisis, I think all around the world banks have become stronger – stronger balance sheets, more capital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think it is fortunate that we went through this period and we now have stronger banks to meet the challenge of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We want to make sure that banks use this balance sheet to be able to help economies, sectors, industries tide through, while maintaining their strength and resilience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That balance needs to be recognised and that balance needs to be struck.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we will continue to track the schemes and make sure that it is processed efficiently and expeditiously.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But unfortunately, they hire quite a number of Singapore workers and want to keep above the water.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: So, is there any way we can assist such companies, which are in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why not give us the details and certainly, MAS and ESG can look into it.
